verdicts.rationale: Story 1 uses the table accurately (2021→2024 case rise, stable 81–84% coverage, per-million comparisons) and ties the numbers to the ~95% herd-immunity threshold. Story 2 misstates the 2022 change as a 3% increase (it was ~68% over 2021), claims 'record high' coverage when 86% in 2018–19 was higher, and asserts unsupported declines in India and Germany.

Story 2 is livelier but misstates the data: the 5x comparison belongs to 2023 (one year prior), not three years prior (2021, where the ratio is ~31x), and the claim that cases were 'steadily decreasing since 2019' with only a 'brief dip in 2020' contradicts the table's 2020-2022 trough. Story 1 sticks to figures the table supports and adds the genuinely useful caveat that the rebound may partly reflect pandemic-era reporting anomalies.

Story 2 is livelier but rests on wrong or unsupported claims — there was no 'steady decline from 2000 to 2011', the 2021-to-2024 jump is roughly 3,000% not 500%, the '70%' drop is misstated, and the vaccination-focus explanation is not in the data. Story 1 describes the same volatility, pandemic dip and 2024 spike accurately, so its factual reliability outweighs Story 2's stylistic edge.

Story 2 is livelier but misstates the data: 2000–2011 was volatile rather than a "steady decline," the 2021→2024 rise is roughly 3,000% not 500%, the "nearly 70%" pandemic drop does not match the 2019–2020 figures, and the vaccination-focus explanation is unsupported. Story 1 stays within the table and still conveys the volatility, pandemic dip, and 2024 spike.

Story 1 accurately identifies the dominant feature of the data — the pandemic dip and the extraordinary 2024 surge to 941,893 cases (137.1 per million) — though it slips in calling 2012 the pre-2024 incidence peak when 2004 was higher at 41.1 per million. Story 2 is flashier but factually broken: the '1371% in five years' misreads the 2024 incidence value, the claimed 45% decline from 2010 to 2023 is actually a slight rise, and it ignores the 2024 spike entirely.

Story 2 is livelier but riddled with fabrications: a 2025 figure of 1,943,893 (actual 265,317), a bogus 900% increase, and a claimed low point in 2010 when the low was 4.6 per million in 2021. Story 1 is plainer but every figure it cites matches the table, making it the more trustworthy and genuinely informative account.

Story 2 is livelier but misstates the baseline as "150,000–175,000" (the series ranges from 116,598 to 250,330) and invents a "late 2024" timeframe the annual data cannot support, while calling a period with 941,893 cases "stubbornly contained" up to that point. Story 1 sticks to figures the table supports, so its accuracy outweighs Story 2's stylistic edge, though both ignore the 2025 fall to 265,317.

Story 1 is livelier but misstates the data: the 2021→2024 rise is roughly 3,000%, not 500%, the 2020 drop is ~54% rather than 'nearly 70%', and the 2000–2011 period was not a steady decline. Story 2 is drier yet every figure and comparison it cites matches the table, so it wins overall despite the flatter prose.

Story 2 is livelier but rests on several claims the table contradicts: no 'steady decline' from 2000–2011, the 2024 peak is roughly a 3,000% rise over 2021 rather than 500%, the '70%' pandemic drop is imprecise, and the vaccination-focus explanation is unsupported. Story 1 is drier yet every figure and trend it states matches the data, which decides the overall verdict.

Both cover the same figures with the same structure and both omit the key insight in the data — the 2019 spike and the 2023–24 resurgence back above 669,000 cases despite flat 83–84% coverage, plus India's high coverage yet higher rate than Germany. Story 2 is livelier but overreaches with claims like 'crushing the virus' and 'eradicating diseases' that the table does not support, so Story 1's more measured accuracy wins overall.

Both stories cover the same figures accurately, but Story 1 adds an unsupported causal attribution to vaccination and sits awkwardly between a 'plummet' headline and a described rebound, while Story 2 states the peak, trough, 2021–2023 rise and incidence decline precisely and coheres better. Story 1 is livelier, but Story 2 is the sounder piece overall.

Story 2 is livelier and its 113% figure checks out, but its centerpiece claim of a 245% rise between 2019 and 2023 is wrong (22,989 to 24,782 is about 8%), and the vaccination-decline explanation is not in the data. Story 1 is plainer but every figure and period it cites matches the table, so accuracy decides it.

Story 2 is livelier but internally contradictory and factually wrong: it says 2021 deaths fell to 103,901 (actually the 2020 figure) while also stating 151,463 died in 2021, and it adds an unsupported claim about rising vaccination rates and expert warnings. Story 1 reports the figures accurately and consistently, which outweighs its flatter prose.

Story 2's headline says '6 Million' and calls 2020 a 'significant drop' when it was a routine yearly decline, and it ignores the latest year (2021), while also conflating the count with a 'mortality rate'. Story 1 reports the full 2000–2021 span with accurate figures and a correct ~43% decline.

Story 1 misstates the post-2010 pace as "just over 4,000 deaths per year" (the actual average is roughly 1,500) and calls the trend "consistent" despite the 2005 uptick, while Story 2's figures (the ~50,000 drop from 2000–2010 and the 29,255→16,265 span) all check out against the table. Both are similarly organized and plainly written, so accuracy decides it.

Story 1 is livelier but makes several unsupported claims — a 'steady decline from 2000 to 2011' contradicted by the 2004 spike, a '500% increase from three years prior' when 2021's 30,402 to 2024's 941,893 is roughly thirtyfold, and speculation about vaccination programs shifting focus. Story 2 stays within the table, adds the incidence figures, and reaches a comparably clear arc, so it wins on accuracy and informativeness while the two are even on structure and readability.

Story 2 is livelier and offers more interpretation, but it misstates a "steady decline from 2000 to 2011" (2004 and 2008–2011 rose), calls the 2021→2024 jump a "500% increase" when it is roughly 3,000%, and adds an unsupported causal claim about vaccination focus. Story 1 has one clear error (the 2000–2019 range is 116,598–250,330, not 199,000–250,000) and a debatable "pre-pandemic" comparison, but is otherwise faithful to the table, so it wins overall on accuracy.

Story 2 is livelier but introduces unsupported specifics — a '150,000–175,000' baseline that misstates the actual 116k–250k range, 'peaks near 250,000 during mid-decade years' (the 250k peaks are 2004 and 2012), and 'in late 2024 alone' for what is annual data. Story 1 characterizes the same surge accurately, so its factual reliability outweighs Story 2's rhetorical flair; both equally ignore the 2025 fall-back.

Story 1 is more colorful but riddled with errors — it calls 2012 'nearly half a million' (it was 250,330), claims the 2024 spike was 'more than six times' any other year (it was under four), and states a range of 69,605–250,330 that contradicts its own mention of 2021's 30,402. Story 2 states every figure and ratio accurately, adds the incidence dimension, and closes its arc cleanly, so it wins on all criteria except raw stylistic flair.

Story 1 is riddled with errors: cases never fell to 'low single digits', the 2024 jump over 2023's 163,400 is roughly 476% not 37%, the 9.9 figure belongs to 2020 not 2023, pandemic years were not 26-40 per million, and it invents claims about lethality and a 'six month' window. Story 2 accurately characterizes the historical range, the 2020-21 trough, the 2024 peak and the 2025 decline, with a clear and appropriately measured arc.
